items.label: A
items.critique: An absurd 50,000-gold offer to buy an inn, 'lad', breezy exclamations and 'stay out of [Person]'s way if you want to stay alive!': the campaign's comic merchant voice.

items.label: B
items.critique: Moral dilemma between chapel and a debtor with literary touches ('The saints have other cups', 'You never spoke to me'); colon and semicolon usage and the hushed tone are not Nox's.

items.label: C
items.critique: Sentimental heirloom ('Thirty years of her hand in it', 'receipt and charm'), a collector rival, and an escape by barge: tidy, symmetrical two-giver dilemma in a literary register.

items.label: D
items.critique: Used-car-salesman joke ('only used it on weekends'), '300 gold or more', 'There ya go!' and a double-dash: unmistakably Westwood's humour and pricing.

items.label: E
items.critique: Official sponsorship, a Chief Engineer, a foul little urchin bothering bats near an apple orchard, a ruby key: plain, quest-mechanical exposition with concrete items and locations.

items.label: F
items.critique: Charter, tolls, a bailiff of a rival lord: political-legal intrigue phrased in measured, balanced sentences with no exclamations or jokes.

items.label: G
items.critique: 'Hail, brave Adventurer!', 'the menfolk of [Place] cannot live without us!' and hungry Ogres with grumbling stomachs: Westwood's hammy, tongue-in-cheek damsels.

items.label: H
items.critique: Eloping lovers and a stolen dowry, a draught 'for the morning after': warm romantic-folk storytelling, quiet and economical, unlike Nox's broad quest-giver lines.

items.label: I
items.critique: Dead-or-alive bounty with a 500 vs 250 gold split, 'despicable scoundrel behind bars!', an unmasked gang nickname and double-dashes: the campaign's bounty shape and voice.

items.label: J
items.critique: A drowned ferryman's widow and an unpaid guild, 'I'll light a candle for you': grief-tinged social realism and semicolon rhythm, not Westwood's register.

tells: Westwood's choices are mechanical and comic (buy or don't, kill or capture for different gold sums, accept or refuse); the new ones are symmetrical moral dilemmas between two sympathetic claimants for one object.
Westwood names exact gold rewards ('500 in gold', '50,000 in gold'); the new texts pay in vague 'silver', 'a share', 'what's in the box'.
Westwood uses exclamations, double-dashes, 'lad', 'young [Class]', 'Hail, brave Adventurer!' and broad jokes; the new texts are quiet, wry and use colons and semicolons.
The new texts load each line with backstory and sentiment (heirlooms, debts, dowries, widows, saints) and literary closing beats; Westwood gives just enough plot to act on.
All five new texts share one invented setting's vocabulary (ford, north road, watchtower, barge, reeve, chapel), which makes them read as a set.
